**Title:** Quadratic air drag, set by shape, mass, radius and air density, governs motion in the simulated laboratory

**Abstract:** I ran 218 of the 300 allowed runs. They covered random objects, vacuum controls, and one-factor-at-a-time variations of every object property and launch setting. In a vacuum, motion is plain projectile motion with g ≈ 9.81 m/s², independent of mass, size and shape. In air, the motion is well described by quadratic drag, F = ½·ρ·Cd·A·v². The effective drag coefficient depends on shape: sphere ≈ 0.47, cube ≈ 1.05, cylinder ≈ 0.82. The drag deceleration scales as ρ·A/m, so the effect depends on a combination of properties (air density, radius, mass and shape). Reflectance, temperature, stripes, hardness and batch showed no detectable effect.

**Methods:** I used three kinds of runs.
- Random objects with default launch settings (40 runs).
- Vacuum controls (air_density = 0) with mass fixed at 1 kg, varying height and launch speed/angle. Their other properties were random, so they also tested whether those properties matter.
- One-factor-at-a-time series in air, with 4–10 replicates each, around a baseline of a 0.3 kg, r = 0.1 m sphere dropped from 40 m. I varied mass, radius, shape, air density, temperature, reflectance, stripes, hardness and batch.
- Extra runs with oblique launches (angles of 45°, −30°, 60° and 0°).

For analysis I compared group means and standard deviations. I then simulated the trajectory with quadratic drag (k = ½ρ·Cd·A/m, with A = πr² for sphere and cylinder and A = (2r)² for cube). I fitted the three Cd values by least squares to the group means of flight_time, impact_speed and distance, weighted by the stated measurement errors.

**Results:**
- **Vacuum:** The 10 m drop gives t ≈ 1.42 s and v ≈ 14.0 m/s, matching g = 9.81 m/s² (√(2gh) = 14.0). The 20 m drop gives 2.02 s and about 19.8 m/s. Mass 1 kg objects with random radius, shape and other properties all agree to within noise. The launch at 10 m/s and 30° gives t ≈ 2.02 s and a range of about 17.5 m, as ballistics predicts.
- **Air, default drop from 10 m:** Heavy, small objects behave nearly as in vacuum. Light, large ones are slowed: the 0.23 kg cube with r = 0.073 m takes 1.58 s and lands at 10.6 m/s, versus 1.43 s and 13.9 m/s in vacuum.
- **Mass (sphere, r = 0.1, 40 m drop):** Heavier objects fall faster in air. The flight time is 3.45 s at 0.3 kg, 3.03 s at 1 kg and 2.91 s at 3 kg. The impact speed is 17.4, 23.7 and 26.3 m/s respectively.
- **Radius (1 kg sphere, 40 m drop):** Larger radius means more drag. The flight time is 2.90 s at r = 0.05, 3.03 s at 0.1 and 3.56 s at 0.2. The impact speed is 26.8, 23.7 and 16.2 m/s.
- **Air density (1 kg sphere, r = 0.1, 40 m drop):** More density means more drag. The flight time is 2.95 s at 0.6, 3.03 s at 1.2 and 3.21 s at 2.4 kg/m³. The impact speed is 25.5, 23.7 and 20.4 m/s.
- **Shape (1 kg, r = 0.1, 40 m drop):** The sphere takes 3.03 s, the cylinder 3.16 s and the cube 3.35 s. Impact speeds are 23.7, 21.0 and 18.4 m/s.
- **Quadratic drag model:** A single model fits all 85 distinct condition groups, including oblique launches, with a normalised residual RMS of about 1.1. This means the fit matches within measurement noise. The fitted coefficients are Cd(sphere) = 0.47, Cd(cube) = 1.05 and Cd(cylinder) = 0.82. The drag deceleration scales as ρ·A/m, so mass, radius, shape and air density act in combination. Mass and radius have no effect in a vacuum.
- **Null effects:** In the 0.3 kg sphere series, temperature (−20 vs 80 °C), reflectance (0 vs 1), stripes (0 vs 10), hardness (1 vs 10) and batch (1 vs 50) all give flight times within about 0.02 s and impact speeds within about 0.1–0.2 m/s of the baseline. This is consistent with noise. No dependence on these five was seen in the vacuum or random runs either.
- **Launch settings:** Height, speed and angle act through ordinary projectile kinematics, with drag on top of that. I did not test the sign of the angle beyond one −30° run; it fit the model.

**Discussion:** The laboratory follows ordinary gravity (g ≈ 9.81 m/s²) plus quadratic air drag. The drag has the form ½ρ·Cd(shape)·A/m·v². Mass, radius, shape, air density, height, speed and angle matter. Reflectance, temperature, stripes, hardness and batch appear irrelevant. The one interaction is that drag depends on the combination ρ·Cd·A/m. Confidence is high for the relevant variables and the quadratic form, and moderate for the exact Cd values.

**Limitations:**
- Cd values are fitted with an assumed projected area. For the cube I assumed (2r)², and for the cylinder πr² (so the cylinder's Cd absorbs any geometry difference). Only the products Cd·A are well determined.
- The exponent of the speed dependence was assumed to be 2 and not fitted freely, although the fit quality supports it.
- Small effects of the "irrelevant" properties below about 1% could be hidden by noise, given small sample sizes of 4–6 runs per level. Interactions of these properties with drag were not checked in detail.
- The range of conditions at extreme combinations (e.g. strongly upward launches in dense air) was sparsely sampled.

import math

def predict(obj, launch):
    m = obj["mass"]
    r = obj["radius"]
    sh = obj["shape"]
    h = launch.get("height", 10)
    v = launch.get("speed", 0)
    ang = launch.get("angle", 0)
    rho = launch.get("air_density", 1.2)
    Cd = {"sphere": 0.47, "cube": 1.05, "cylinder": 0.82}[sh]
    A = (2 * r) ** 2 if sh == "cube" else math.pi * r * r
    k = 0.5 * rho * Cd * A / m
    g = 9.81
    a = math.radians(ang)
    vx = v * math.cos(a)
    vy = v * math.sin(a)
    x = 0.0
    y = h
    t = 0.0
    dt = 0.002
    while y > 0:
        s = math.hypot(vx, vy)
        ax = -k * s * vx
        ay = -g - k * s * vy
        vxn = vx + ax * dt
        vyn = vy + ay * dt
        yn = y + vyn * dt
        if yn <= 0:
            f = y / (y - yn) if y != yn else 1.0
            x += vxn * dt * f
            t += dt * f
            vx, vy = vxn, vyn
            y = yn
            break
        x += vxn * dt
        y = yn
        vx, vy = vxn, vyn
        t += dt
    return {"flight_time": t, "distance": x, "impact_speed": math.hypot(vx, vy)}

I'm designing a systematic set of experiments to isolate how mass, radius, shape, air density, temperature, and reflectance each affect drag - varying one parameter at a time while holding others fixed, planning around 60+ runs covering shape variations at fixed mass/radius, radius sweeps, density sweeps, mass sweeps, and temperature extremes to build a cleaner drag model from the data.

You are a scientist studying how objects move in a simulated physics laboratory. The laws of physics in this laboratory may differ from those of the real world. No dataset is given to you: you collect your own data by running experiments, and you analyse it with your own code.

Your task:
1. Design experiments and collect data
2. Analyze the data thoroughly
3. Identify which properties of an object and which launch settings affect its motion
4. Determine the form of each effect, including whether any effect depends on a combination of properties
5. Write a short research paper reporting your findings
6. Submit your law as a Python function that predicts the outcome of an experiment

Your paper MUST include:
- Title
- Abstract (3-5 sentences)
- Methods section: How did you collect your data, and how did you analyze it?
- Results section: What affects the motion, in what way, and how strongly?
- Discussion: What laws govern this laboratory? Which properties matter and which don't?
- Limitations: What caveats apply to your analysis?

Be specific about:
- Which properties and settings you consider to have an effect, and which you consider irrelevant
- The form and size of each effect
- Whether any effect depends on a combination of properties
- Your confidence level in your findings

Important: Base your conclusions ONLY on the data you collect. Report findings honestly, including if you find no effect.

Please study the following laboratory and write a research paper about your findings.

## The laboratory
In each run an object is released or thrown. The laboratory measures how long it takes to reach the ground (flight_time, in s), how far it travels horizontally before landing (distance, in m) and its speed when it lands (impact_speed, in m/s). Measurements include a small random error, independent for every measurement, with a standard deviation of 0.01 s for flight_time and 1% of the true value for distance and impact_speed.

Object properties:
- mass: 0.1 to 10 kg
- radius: 0.02 to 0.2 m
- shape: sphere, cube or cylinder
- reflectance: 0 (black) to 1 (white)
- temperature: -20 to 80 °C
- stripes: 0 to 10 (number of painted stripes)
- hardness: 1 to 10
- batch: 1 to 50 (production batch)

Launch settings:
- height: 0.5 to 50 m (default 10)
- speed: 0 to 20 m/s (default 0)
- angle: -90 to 90 degrees, where 0 is horizontal and 90 is straight up (default 0)
- air_density: 0 (vacuum) to 2.4 kg/m^3 (default 1.2)

In a run you may set any object properties and any launch settings. Object properties you do not set are those of an object taken at random from the laboratory's stock; launch settings you do not set take their default values. Every run records all properties, all settings and the three measurements.

## Budget
300 runs in total, at most 100 runs per turn, and at most 12 turns.

## What you can do in each turn
Your reply may contain experiments, Python code, or both.

Experiments go inside <experiments></experiments> as a JSON array. Each experiment is a number of runs with the same settings, for example:
- {"object": {"mass": 2, "shape": "cube"}, "launch": {"height": 30, "air_density": 0}, "n": 10}: 10 runs dropping a 2 kg cube from 30 m in a vacuum, its other properties random
- {"n": 50}: 50 runs with random objects and the default launch settings

You analyse your data with your own Python code, inside <python></python>. Each block runs in a fresh Python 3.12 process with numpy, pandas, scipy, statsmodels and scikit-learn installed and no internet access. All runs collected so far are already loaded in the pandas DataFrame `df`, with one column for each property, setting and measurement, plus run and set (what you set in that run, for example "temperature=70; height=30", empty if you set nothing). Only what your code prints comes back to you, up to 8000 characters per block; figures are not shown. Each block may run for up to 60 seconds. There is no limit on the number of blocks in a reply.

Experiments in a reply are carried out before its code. After each reply you will see the new runs and the output of your code. Anything else you write in a reply is kept as your notes.

## Finishing
When you are done, or when your turns run out, write your paper inside <report></report>. A reply that contains a report ends the study, and nothing else in it is carried out. You will then be asked for your law.

Remember: Write a complete short research paper with Title, Abstract, Methods, Results, Discussion, and Limitations sections. Be specific about which properties and settings matter, the form and size of their effects, and any effect that depends on a combination of properties.
